messages.subject: genetic map vs physical map
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I'm using qtl2 on a MAGIC population where I have a genetic and physical map (~32,000 snps). Many markers in the genetic map share the same cM. I'd like to compare the output from using just the genetic map (as outlined in the user guide) versus just the physical map.

Here's my code for using the genetic map:
allpheno <- read_cross2("AllDiscs.yaml")
pr <- calc_genoprob(allpheno, error_prob=0.002)
apr <- genoprob_to_alleleprob(pr)
k <- calc_kinship(apr, "loco")
out <- scan1(apr, allpheno$pheno, k)

How can I do the same using the physical map?

Thanks,
Elsa

messages.body_plain:
In calc_genoprob() attempt to reconstruct founder genotypes from the observed SNP data. This requires an understanding of the rate of recombination in each marker interval along the chromosome, which is where the genetic map is used. The physical map is not a suitable replacement.

If you just want to plot the results relative to physical distance rather than relative to genetic distance, you could use

   plot(allpheno$pmap, out)

where you might have used

  plot(allpheno$gmap, out)

karl

messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

I am working on genetic mapping in a DO cohort and have been attempting to perform mediation analysis for a particular protein that I believe is causal for a LOD peak.

The way in which I have been doing this is as follows:
Add the protein abundance as a covariate in the cross2 object
Recalculate the genoprobs and alleleprobs
Use the alleleprobs object in scan1() and plot the output

Strangely, there was no effect on the LOD peaks after I had completed this process. I tried adding the covariate matrix explicitly into scan1 as well with addcovar, although this had no effect.

To test whether the covariates were having any effect, I removed all of the covariates (ngen, cage number and protein abundance) and recalculated files again. This had no effect on the scan1 output either. Please find attached screenshots of the scan1 outputs (grey is without covariates and blue is with).

Would you please be able to explain what is going wrong here?

Kind regards,

Harry

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Harry,

When I've worked with data from DO mice, I've used batch covariates coded as a collection of binary indicator variables for all but one level of a factor. So, if I had k cages, I would use k-1 binary covariates. The i'th cage covariate, then, would have a one for the mice in cage i and zero for mice in other cages.

If your cage covariate is a single character vector, cage_number, with distinct values corresponding to distinct cages, one way to code this in R is:

cage_number <- rep(paste0("cage", 1:4), each = 4)
# i define above cage_number for illustration. you would just use your character vector and omit this line
unique(cage_number) -> levels
cage_binaries <- sapply(FUN = function(x)as.numeric(cage_number == x), X = as.list(levels))
cage_binaries

You could then use cage_binaries as an additive covariates matrix in calls to qtl2::scan1. Because qtl2::scan1 checks addcovar for linear independence and chooses a subset of columns that is linearly independent while maintaining the rank of the inputted matrix, you can actually input the full cage_binaries matrix without needing to first remove a column.

I believe that intcovar is for covariates that you wish to assess for genotype by covariate interactions, but I have less experience with that input.

In other words, I believe that qtl2::scan1, when called with non-NULL intcovar, models the trait Y as

Y = (founder allele probabilities) + intcovar + intcovar * (founder allele probabilities) + epsilon

when you don't input a kinship matrix. If you input a kinship matrix, then you end up fitting the corresponding mixed effects model.

I hope that this helps.

fred

messages.subject: backcrosses in two directions
messages.body_plain:
Is there a way to analyze backcrosses in two different directions at the same time? I am doing QTL mapping in sawflies which are haplodiploid. From preliminary data different traits had dominance in opposite directions, but intercrosses were not feasible, so we backcrossed in both directions.

The workaround I have thought of is to code the cross design as an intercross and make all of the chromosomes X chromosomes. All of the individuals in the mapping population are female, and in haplodiploids all of the chromosomes act as an X chromosome (diploid in the female and haploid in the male). We backcrossed hybrid females to pure males to generate backcross females. Genetically this should be identical to an intercross with a hybrid male on the X chromosome. Is it possible to code more than one chromosome as an X?

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] backcrosses in two directions
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl2 doesn't currently include any facilities for the combined analysis of multiple crosses, such as a pair of backcrosses. So you're on your own at present.

You can in principle have multiple X chromosomes, but it seems that the input format doesn't allow it. But you can switch the non-X chromosomes to act like an X chromosome after reading in the data:

  mycross <- read_cross2("mycross.yaml")
  mycross$is_x_chr[ !mycross$is_x_chr ] <- TRUE

karl

messages.subject: 'cores' argument
messages.body_plain:
Dear Carl,

I've been bench marking the time it takes for me to run a genome scan (scan1) by increase the number of cores that I want to use. I was quite surprised to find that the quickest was running on 1 core. In short, I ran scan1 with one phenotype and then increasing the number of cores. I got the following times:
1 core 1 phenotype: 29 sec
2 cores 1 phenotype: 46 sec
10 cores 1 phenotype: 2 min 51 sec.

Is this something you have seen before and are aware of?

I'm doing the analysis on a 32-core processor with 128 GB RAM.

Thanks in advance!
Soren
